title: Deep in one: Proverbs
for: I want wisdom for daily life
subtitle: Eight sessions in the Bible's book of wisdom for ordinary days: what a proverb is, the fear of the LORD, words, work, money, friends and anger, and the wisdom that has a face.
intro: Proverbs is the most practical book in the Bible. It talks about what you say at dinner, how you treat the person who owes you money, whether you get out of bed, who your friends are and what you do with your temper. It is also a book about God, and it never lets the two come apart: wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD, and the fear of the LORD shows itself on an ordinary Tuesday afternoon.

This track reads Proverbs by its own themes rather than chapter by chapter, because most of the book is short sayings gathered without an outline. Each session opens a chapter in the Study Bible with its notes in plain words, and most also open a guide for daily life. Read slowly. A proverb is meant to be turned over in the mind for a week, not finished in a minute. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Deep in one: Proverbs. The group meets eight times and reads the book by its themes: what a proverb is, the fear of the LORD, Wisdom and Folly, words, work, money, friends and anger, and the woman of strength. It suits people who have never read Proverbs and people who have only ever met it as a verse on a calendar. The leader's task is to keep the group in the sayings, to resist turning them into rules or promises, and to let them reach the ordinary week each person lives.

Each person reads the chapter, its notes and the session before the group meets. The meeting reads the key sayings aloud and talks them over, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, small enough that everyone speaks. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for eight meetings, and keep the end time you promised. A leader doesn't need to be wiser than the group. A leader needs to have read the sayings and their notes, and to be willing to say when a proverb has not matched their own life.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit round a table if you can, with Proverbs open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone. Proverbs was written to be remembered, so read the sayings aloud more than once. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about their own homes, money and friendships stays in the room, and that no one has to share a number or a name.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Ten minutes: read the key chapter or sayings aloud, sharing the reading, and let a minute of quiet follow.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is in the text.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse to keep, and the group says what it noticed in it.
Ten minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words.
Five minutes: name the next session and the page it opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Proverbs raises hard questions because life doesn't always follow it. A parent will ask about the child who departed from the way, someone will ask why the diligent person is still poor, someone will ask whether a verse promised them an outcome God didn't give. When that comes, read the note on the saying together, and remember with the group that a proverb describes how things usually go and is not a guarantee. Job and Ecclesiastes are in the Bible for exactly these questions.

Some sayings about the rod, about wives, about kings and about the poor need to be read in their own world before they are applied in ours. Say plainly where Christians read a saying in more than one way, give each reading its strongest form, and never use a proverb to justify harm.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Proverbs touches the places where people hurt most: money trouble, a child who has walked away, a friendship broken by anger, harsh words at home. When someone speaks of that, stop the discussion and listen. Thank them for saying it, don't hand them a proverb as a fix, and don't suggest that their trouble proves they were foolish. Ask whether they would like the group to go on or to pause, and speak with them on their own afterwards.

If someone says that a partner, a parent, a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. On money, debt and law, the group can share wisdom but is not giving financial or legal advice, and it is kind to say so.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: debt or money fear that has taken their sleep, anger at home that has made anyone afraid, drinking that is hard to control, harm done to them at home or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: What a proverb is, and what it is not
teaching: A proverb is a short saying that makes a pattern in life visible. The Hebrew word, mashal, means a comparison, one thing set beside another so that you can see it. Proverbs are true the way a good doctor's advice is true. They describe how God's world usually works, and they are meant to be weighed and applied with judgment, not claimed as guarantees. The book shows this itself, setting two sayings side by side: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you yourself will be like him. Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes” (Proverbs 26:4-5). Both are true. Wisdom is knowing which one this fool needs.

Reading a proverb as a promise has hurt people. Parents who raised a child with care have read that a child trained in the way he should go will not depart from it, and blamed themselves, or God, when the child walked away. The saying describes the usual fruit of faithful parenting. It doesn't hand any parent control of another person's heart. The same book that says diligent hands bring wealth knows that the poor are often wronged, and Job and Ecclesiastes stand beside Proverbs in the Bible to say what happens when the pattern breaks. Wisdom holds all three.

sessions.question: Is there a proverb, from the Bible or anywhere else, that you have treated as a promise, and what happened when life didn't follow it?
sessions.do: Read Proverbs 26:1 to 12 slowly. Choose one saying and write down a situation where it would be wise to follow it and one where it would not.

verse.text: For the LORD gives wisdom; from His mouth come knowledge and understanding.

group.open: What is a saying your parents or grandparents repeated that turned out to be true, or turned out to be wrong?
discuss: Proverbs 26:4 and 26:5 seem to contradict each other. What does setting them side by side teach about wisdom?
Where have you seen a proverb used as a promise, and what did it do to the person who believed it?
Why might God have put Job and Ecclesiastes in the Bible beside Proverbs?
group.pray: Ask God for the wisdom to know which saying fits which moment, and pray for any parent in the group carrying a child who has walked away.

sessions.title: Proverbs 1 and the fear of the LORD
teaching: Proverbs states its purpose in its opening lines: wisdom and instruction, prudence for the simple, knowledge and discretion for the young. Then it gives its motto: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and discipline” (Proverbs 1:7). The fear of the LORD isn't terror. It is reverence and awe that show themselves in trust and obedience, the posture of a creature who knows the difference between itself and its Maker. And the beginning here means more than the place you start and then leave behind. It is the first principle, the ground everything else in the book stands on.

This is why Proverbs refuses to separate the spiritual from the practical. Its sayings about honest scales and kindness to the poor aren't a secular supplement to faith. They are what the fear of the LORD looks like in a marketplace. Israel's neighbours had wisdom writing too, and Proverbs shares some of its forms and sayings, but it sets all of it under the LORD's name. Chapter 1 then warns a son against the gang that lies in wait for blood, and brings on Wisdom calling in the streets. Every reader is addressed as that son, taught by a parent who wants him to live.

open.label: Proverbs 1, passage by passage
open.why: The purpose of Proverbs, its motto in verse 7, the warning against the violent gang and Wisdom's first call, explained in plain words.

also.label: The fear of the LORD
also.why: What the whole Bible says about the fear of the LORD, gathered for anyone trying to understand what it means and why it matters.

also.label: The fear of God
also.why: The fear of God as a doctrine: reverence, awe and trust, traced from Proverbs and the Psalms into the New Testament.

also.label: Did Proverbs borrow from Egyptian wisdom?
also.why: Whether Proverbs borrowed from Egyptian wisdom writing, and what it means that Israel set shared wisdom under the LORD's name.

sessions.question: If the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, where in your ordinary week does it most need to begin?
sessions.do: Write Proverbs 1:7 on a card and carry it this week. Each evening, name one decision you made that day and ask whether reverence for God shaped it.

verse.text: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, but fools despise wisdom and discipline.

group.open: Who was the wisest person you knew growing up, and what made them wise?
discuss: What is the difference between fearing God and being afraid of him?
Proverbs puts honest business and kindness to the poor under the fear of the LORD. What would change if you saw your own work that way?
The book speaks to every reader as a son or daughter being taught. Why is that a good way to come to it, at any age?
group.pray: Ask God for a reverent heart that trusts him, and give thanks for the people who taught each of you wisdom when you were young.

care: If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Proverbs 8 and 9, Lady Wisdom and Lady Folly
teaching: Proverbs pictures wisdom as a woman calling at the city gates and the crossroads, offering what silver and gold can't buy. In chapter 8 she says she was there before the world began, beside the LORD as he marked out the heavens and set a boundary for the sea. Then chapter 9 sets two women in front of every passer-by. Wisdom has built her house, prepared her table and sent out her servants to invite the simple. Folly sits at her own door, loud and naive, offering stolen water and bread eaten in secret. The two call out with nearly the same words. The difference is where each meal leads.

The church has long heard Christ in chapter 8. Paul calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and the New Testament speaks of the Son as the one through whom all things were made. In the fourth century Arius leaned on Proverbs 8:22, which speaks of wisdom as made by the LORD, to argue that the Son was a creature, and the council at Nicaea in 325 rejected his teaching. The poem personifies a quality of God, and it is wise not to press every line as a statement about the Son. But its shape, a delight beside God at creation who calls people to life, finds its fullest face in Jesus.

open.why: Wisdom's call at the gates and her place beside God at creation, explained in plain words with how Christians have read the chapter.

also.label: Proverbs 9, the guided study
also.why: Walk through Proverbs 9 in seven steps and set the invitations of Wisdom and Folly side by side, line by line.

also.label: Nicaea to Chalcedon
also.why: How the councils that wrote the creeds answered Arius, who leaned on Proverbs 8 to call the Son a creature.

sessions.question: Wisdom and Folly both invite you to dinner. Which invitation sounds more appealing to you this week, and why?
sessions.do: Read Proverbs 9 aloud. Write the two invitations side by side, and next to each, what it is offering you in your own life right now.

verse.text: For whoever finds me finds life and obtains the favor of the LORD.

group.open: What is the best invitation you have ever received?
discuss: Folly's invitation sounds almost the same as Wisdom's. Why does that make it dangerous?
What does it add to think of wisdom as a person calling out, rather than a set of rules?
Christians have heard Christ in Proverbs 8. Where does that reading help, and where should it be held with care?
group.pray: Give thanks that wisdom calls out in public places to anyone who will listen, and ask for ears to hear her voice above the voice of Folly.

sessions.title: Words and the tongue
teaching: Few subjects come up more often in Proverbs than speech. The book knows that words build and destroy: “Life and death are in the power of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit” (Proverbs 18:21). It warns against the liar, the flatterer, the gossip and the person who answers before listening, and it praises the word fitly spoken, the gentle answer and the friend whose honest rebuke is worth more than an enemy's kisses. Most of its sayings on speech aren't about grand speeches. They are about the conversation at the kitchen table and the remark passed on at work.

Proverbs also prizes silence. “When words are many, sin is unavoidable, but he who restrains his lips is wise” (Proverbs 10:19). The wise person is often the one who says less, waits longer, and checks whether a thing is true before repeating it. James would later write that no one can tame the tongue, and Proverbs doesn't pretend it is easy. But it does assume that the tongue follows the heart. Changing what you say starts further down, with what you love and what you fear.

open.label: Proverbs 18, passage by passage
open.why: Proverbs 18 on the tongue, the listening ear, and the power of words to give life or bring death, explained in plain words.

also.label: The Wisdom Books explorer
also.why: Gather every saying in Proverbs on words and the tongue, and read them together in one place.

also.label: Gossip and the tongue
also.why: What the whole Bible says about gossip and the tongue, for someone trying to change the way they speak.

sessions.question: Whose words have given you life, and whose words do you need to stop repeating?
sessions.do: For one week, before you pass on anything about someone who isn't in the room, ask whether it is true, whether it is kind, and whether it is yours to say. Notice how often you stop.

verse.text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

group.open: What is a sentence someone said to you years ago that you still remember?
discuss: Proverbs says life and death are in the power of the tongue. Where have you seen words do either?
Why does the book praise silence so often? When has saying less been the wisest thing you did?
If speech follows the heart, what does that mean for anyone trying to change how they talk?
group.pray: Ask God to guard each person's mouth this week, and pray by name for someone whose words have hurt or helped you.

care: James does not treat cruel words lightly, and neither should anyone who has been on the receiving end of them. Words can do real harm. If anger has become something you cannot control, or if anger at home has made anyone afraid, that is more than a verse can fix. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Work and laziness
teaching: Proverbs sends the slacker to school with an ant: “Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise” (Proverbs 6:6). The ant has no commander and still gathers in summer what it will need later. The slacker in Proverbs is a comic figure. He says there's a lion in the street, he turns on his bed like a door on its hinges, and he buries his hand in the dish and is too tired to lift it back to his mouth. The humour has a point. Laziness rarely calls itself laziness. It always has a reason.

The book honours skilled and faithful work, and it says that a person skilled in his work will stand before kings. Work in Proverbs is more than a way to earn. It is part of living wisely in God's world, a share in the order he made. But Proverbs never treats hard work as the whole of wisdom. It warns against wearing yourself out to get rich, and it says the LORD's blessing adds no sorrow to it. Between the slacker and the person who can never stop stands the ant, working in its season, trusting the God who made the seasons.

also.why: A guide to work and calling, for anyone who wants to see their daily work as part of serving God.

also.why: Practical steps for seeing ordinary work, paid or unpaid, as something offered to God.

also.label: Procrastination and laziness
also.why: What the Bible says about procrastination and laziness, gathered for anyone who keeps putting things off.

sessions.question: Are you more tempted to be the slacker or the person who can never stop working, and what does each one trust instead of God?
sessions.do: Choose one task you have been putting off and do it first thing tomorrow. Then choose one evening this week to stop work completely, and notice which is harder.

verse.text: Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise.

group.open: What was your first job, and what did it teach you?
discuss: The slacker always has a reason. Which excuses do you find most convincing in your own life?
Proverbs praises skilled work. Where have you seen work done so well that it honoured God?
How do you tell the difference between diligence and a restlessness that can't stop?
group.pray: Give thanks for the work each person has, paid or unpaid, and pray for anyone in the group who is out of work or worn out by it.

sessions.title: Money and generosity
teaching: Proverbs talks about money often and without embarrassment. It praises honest weights and condemns dishonest scales. It warns against putting up security for a stranger's debt. It knows that wealth makes friends and that it can grow wings and fly away like an eagle. Some of its sayings make diligence sound like a road to riches, and read alone they could be bent into a promise of prosperity. But the same book says a little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with turmoil, and it calls kindness to the poor a loan to the LORD.

The most searching money prayer in the Bible is in chapter 30, where Agur asks for neither poverty nor riches, only the bread that is his portion. He sees danger on both sides: “Otherwise, I may have too much and deny You” (Proverbs 30:9), or be poor and steal. That prayer cuts against the hope that more money would settle things. Proverbs pairs it with an open hand: the one who refreshes others will be refreshed, and the one who shuts his ears to the cry of the poor will cry out and not be answered. Money is a test of the heart long before it is a measure of success.

also.why: A guide to money and the heart, and how a Christian can hold money with an open hand.

also.why: Practical first steps for giving generously, whatever you earn, and making giving a settled habit.

also.label: Can a Christian be rich?
also.why: An essay on whether a Christian can be rich, and what Scripture asks of anyone who has more than enough.

sessions.question: Agur prays for neither poverty nor riches. Could you pray that prayer honestly, and what would make it hard?
sessions.do: Look at your spending for the last month and name one way it shows trust in God and one way it shows trust in money. Then give something away this week, quietly, to someone in need.

verse.text: Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender.

group.open: What did your family teach you about money, out loud or without words?
discuss: Some proverbs sound as if faithfulness always brings wealth. How do you read them beside the sayings about the poor being wronged?
Agur is wary of both too much and too little. Which danger is closer to you?
Proverbs calls kindness to the poor a loan to the LORD. What would it look like to take that seriously this month?
group.pray: Pray for anyone in the group under money strain, and ask God for open hands and contented hearts, whatever each person has.

care: If you gave money under pressure, or because you were promised a return, that was not your failure. If it still weighs on you, please talk with a pastor or friend you trust. These notes are not financial advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Friends, anger and pride
teaching: Proverbs is a book about companions. “He who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed” (Proverbs 13:20). A friend loves at all times, the wounds of a friend are faithful, and as iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another. Friendship in Proverbs is a loyalty more than a mood, and it includes the hard word spoken in love. The book is just as clear about the companions to avoid: the hot-tempered, the gossip, the flatterer whose kisses are deceitful. The people you walk with will shape the person you become, and Proverbs wants you to choose them on purpose.

Anger and pride are the two things most likely to ruin a friendship. “He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city” (Proverbs 16:32). Proverbs doesn't say anger is always wrong. It says the fool vents all of it and the wise hold it back. Pride is harder to see, because it hides inside our own judgment. Pride goes before destruction, the book says, and with humility comes wisdom. The person who can't be corrected can't be taught, and in the end can't be a friend.

also.label: Why is pride the root of every other sin?
also.why: A guide to pride and humility, and what humility looks like in ordinary life and ordinary friendships.

also.label: How to deal with anger
also.why: Practical steps for dealing with anger before it damages the people you love.

also.label: How to build deep friendships as an adult
also.why: Practical steps for making and keeping the kind of friends Proverbs describes, when adult life works against it.

sessions.question: Who in your life has loved you enough to wound you with the truth, and when did you last do that for someone?
sessions.do: Name one friend who sharpens you and tell them so this week. Then name one person you are angry with, and decide before you next see them what you will hold back.

verse.text: As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another.

group.open: Who is the friend you have known longest, and how did you meet?
discuss: Proverbs says a friend's wounds are faithful. What makes a hard word from a friend different from criticism?
The fool vents all his anger and the wise hold it back. Is holding anger back the same as burying it?
Why might pride make a person impossible to befriend and impossible to teach?
group.pray: Give thanks for faithful friends, pray for a friendship that anger or pride has broken, and ask God for a humble and teachable heart.

care: If anger has become something you cannot control, or if anger at home has made anyone afraid, that is more than a verse can fix. Please talk to someone you trust, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

sessions.title: Proverbs 31 and the wisdom that points to Christ
teaching: The book ends with a poem about a woman of strength, an acrostic in which each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The Hebrew phrase, eshet chayil, uses a word for strength and valour, and the same phrase is used of Ruth, a foreign widow. The woman of chapter 31 works, trades, plans, provides, opens her hands to the poor and speaks with wisdom and kindness. Many women have heard the poem as a checklist they could never meet. Read in its place, it is something else: Lady Wisdom of chapters 1 to 9 now living in an ordinary house, the book's whole teaching given a life. And it closes with reverence for the LORD, where the book began.

Proverbs leaves a question it can't answer by itself. Who has ever lived the wisdom it describes? Solomon gathered the sayings and did not keep them. Jesus grew in wisdom as a boy, taught in proverbs and parables, and said that someone greater than Solomon was here. Paul calls him the one “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). The wisdom of Proverbs isn't finally a technique for a successful life. It has a face, and it calls you, as it always did, to come and eat at its table. The other tracks of the Academy carry that question on through the rest of Scripture.

also.why: Wisdom as a doctrine, from the fear of the LORD in Proverbs to Christ, the wisdom of God, in the New Testament.

sessions.question: Who have you known whose ordinary life made wisdom visible, and what did you learn from watching them?
sessions.do: Read Proverbs 31:10 to 31 and then Proverbs 9:1 to 6. Note what the woman of strength and Lady Wisdom share, and where you see that same wisdom lived out by Jesus.

verse.text: She opens her mouth with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue.

group.open: Of all the people you have known, whose character would you most like to share?
discuss: The poem of Proverbs 31 has often been heard as a checklist. What changes when it is read as wisdom given a life?
Solomon gathered the proverbs and did not keep them. What does that tell you about the limits of good advice?
Jesus said someone greater than Solomon was here. How does seeing Christ as wisdom change the way you read Proverbs?
group.pray: Give thanks for the people whose lives have shown each of you wisdom, and ask Christ, the wisdom of God, to form his life in each of you.

care: If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
